title: The Vow Before Indra
subtitle: Krishna returns the Parijata to heaven
story:
When the Parijata returned to the city of the celestials, it was more than a tree coming home. It was the same tree that had nearly set brother against brother — the battle over it had ended only when Kashyapa and Aditi, sent by Brahma, halted the fight, and the two who had quarrelled bathed in the Jahnvi and made peace. Now Krishna carried the tree back up from Dwaraka after a year of festival, and in heaven he saluted Indra, Aditi and Kashyapa, one after another — the gesture of a son arriving at his parents' door, the heavenly tree settling back into the garden it had left. The court that had seen them fight now saw them stand together before their parents, and the sight carried its own peace.

Aditi received it exactly that way. After Krishna had bowed to her, she spoke. "May you both always entertain such brotherly feeling," she said. "O Janardana, you are to satisfy this desire of mine."

"It shall be so," said Krishna.

Then, having honored his parents, he turned to the king of gods, and his words changed the mood of the meeting. "O king of gods, giver of honor," he said, "I have been commanded by the high-souled Shiva to destroy all the unslayable Danavas who live on earth. From today, within ten days, I will kill all those Asuras. At the time of that battle, Pravara, together with the heroic Jayanta, must wait in the sky to slay the Danavas. Of them, one is a god in human form, and the other is the son of a god."

It was a strange vow, and Indra knew why it was strange. These Danavas were unslayable by the gods. They carried a boon from Brahma, and no weapon of heaven could touch them; that was why they had lived so long on earth, proud and untroubled. Yet here was Krishna promising to finish them within ten days, and asking that the two sons of the gods stand ready in the sky when he did — waiting, as though the slaughter of the invincible were a thing that could be scheduled. The gods gathered closer at the words, for it was not every day that the lord who lived among mortals set a date for war. Indra had long known these Danavas as a burden heaven could not lift; now, for the first time, he heard someone promise to lift it.

Krishna explained it plainly. "Although those Danavas, proud of the boon conferred on them by Brahma, cannot be killed by the gods," he said, "we will kill them, for I am now a man."

There was the whole secret, and it turned the vow from a boast into a promise. The boon that shielded the Danavas from every god left them helpless against a man — and Krishna, who had just spent a year being bound with garlands and ransomed with cows, spoke of that human form as his weapon. He was the man who would do what heaven could not, and the gods had only to watch the sky when the killing began.

Indra, pleased, answered, "So it will be." And then the king of gods and the lord of Dwaraka embraced each other — the quarrel over the Parijata finished, at last, with an embrace; and a different war agreed upon in the same breath, one to be fought on earth within ten days. And somewhere below, on the earth he had chosen, the Danavas went on living as though no such promise existed. The ten days had begun to run, and the world below did not yet know it.
reflection: The vow's logic is the striking thing: the Danavas' invincibility is a gift from Brahma, and it is precisely that gift which makes them killable — by a man. Krishna speaks of his human form not as a weakness but as the one door the boon left open, and the embrace with Indra seals both reconciliation and war in a single moment.
next_story_tease: Within those ten days, Krishna would be drawn to a sacrifice at Shatpura where the Danavas were already making demands.
hero_scene: Krishna before Indra in the celestial city, one hand resting on the returned Parijata tree, as he vows to destroy the Danavas within ten days while Indra listens and Aditi looks on.
